visits.text: Four lighthouses for a single hazard: on the Calf of Man and offshore, all mark the rocks of Chicken Rock. The first two, a matching pair, date from 1818. In 1875, a lighthouse built on the rock itself replaced them; you will see it offshore. The fourth was added on the Calf in 1968, after a fire at Chicken Rock. Allow time for the walk: the boat leaves at the agreed time.

activities.text: You will board a boat at Port St Mary for the Calf of Man, a 2.5 km² island managed as a nature reserve. Along the way, the boat passes rocks sculpted by the sea, such as the Drinking Dragon, whose name evokes a dragon drinking. On day trips, you have about three hours ashore after landing. Gray seals live along the coast. The Manx shearwater, a seabird named after the island, had nearly disappeared because of rats. Its population has now recovered to around 1,000 pairs.

days_plan.itin_title: Isle of Man in 4 days: Laxey, Snaefell, Peel, and Castletown

visits.text: Castle Rushen looks impregnable, yet Robert the Bruce, King of Scotland, captured it in 1313 after a three-week siege. This limestone castle ranks among the best-preserved medieval castles in the British Isles. It later served as a prison until 1891. Look up at the clock: Queen Elizabeth I gave it in 1597, and it still works. Open from late March to early November, £14 per adult.

activities.text: You will finish with a guided heritage tour of Castletown, the island’s capital until 1869. It starts at the Old Grammar School, a chapel built around 1200 that later became a school, described as the island’s oldest roofed building. It takes in the Old House of Keys, where the House of Keys, the elected chamber of parliament, sat from 1821 to 1874. It also includes the Nautical Museum, an 18th-century captain’s house with its boathouse. Allow 2 hours, on Wednesdays and Saturdays, by reservation.

days_plan.itin_title: Isle of Man in 4 days: Laxey, Snaefell, Peel, and Castletown

visits.text: Cregneash is a former village of small-scale farmers that became a living museum in 1938. Its thatched cottages show what rural Manx life was like in the 19th century. Manx, the island’s Celtic language, remained in everyday use here longer than elsewhere. Ned Maddrell, often described as its last native speaker, grew up here. In the meadows, look for Loaghtan sheep, which have brown wool and usually four horns. The village is open from late March to early November, from 10 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.

If you have binoculars, take them out at The Sound, the island’s southwestern tip, very close to Cregneash. Opposite, across a channel called Calf Sound, lies the Calf of Man. Between the two, Kitterland Rock often serves as a resting spot for seals. The café here offers panoramic views and is open year-round: have lunch there before taking the boat.

days_plan.itin_title: Isle of Man in 4 days: Laxey, Snaefell, Peel, and Castletown

visits.text: The best starting point is the Manx Museum, where admission is free (a donation is suggested but optional). An introductory film summarizes 10,000 years of the island’s history. The Viking gallery displays silver and gold treasures unearthed on the island. Another section of the museum tells the story of the Tourist Trophy, or TT, the motorcycle race held every year on the island’s roads. The museum is open daily from 9:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., and mornings are quieter.

The scent of sea air and the cries of gulls accompany you along Douglas Promenade, which follows the curve of the bay. Out on the water, the Tower of Refuge looks like a small castle. Built in 1832 on Conister Rock, it sheltered shipwrecked sailors, providing bread, water, and a bell to call for help. Admire it from shore: the rock is only accessible on foot at exceptionally low tides, and the crossing is dangerous.

Frank Matcham designed more than 90 theaters, and the Gaiety Theatre in Douglas, which opened in 1900, is among the best preserved. Beneath the stage lies a Corsican trap. This mechanism raises an actor through the floor with a sliding motion, creating the illusion of an apparition. The theater describes it as the only known example. Guided tours are offered from April through October by reservation and last up to 2 hours 15 minutes.

If a flag is flying on Douglas Head, the Great Union Camera Obscura is open. This small building dating from 1892 works like a giant camera. On the roof, eleven sets of mirrors and lenses project moving, full-color images of the harbor and bay onto a round table in a darkened room. Volunteers open it mainly on summer weekend afternoons, with admission costing £3. Even without visiting the camera obscura, the hill offers sweeping views of the bay.

activities.text: Next, ride along the waterfront on the Douglas Bay Horse Tramway, a horse-drawn tram. Opened in 1876, it is the world’s last 19th-century horse tramway still in service. It celebrates its 150th anniversary in 2026. Trams run from April to early November, generally every half hour. Board near the Villa Marina and get off at Derby Castle, where the Manx Electric Railway departs for Laxey.

days_plan.itin_title: Isle of Man in 4 days: Laxey, Snaefell, Peel, and Castletown

visits.text: The Great Laxey Wheel, nicknamed Lady Isabella, is the largest working waterwheel in the world. Its 22-meter diameter matches the height of a seven-story building. Built in 1854, it pumped out water flooding the Laxey lead and zinc mine. Climb the 95 steps to the platform at the top, then follow the miners’ trail. The site is open from late March to early November, generally from 9:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., with admission costing £14 per adult.

From the outside, Laxey Woollen Mills looks like a woolen goods store; inside, weaving still takes place. The mill was founded in 1881 with the support of English writer John Ruskin. It weaves Manx tartan and undyed wool cloth from Loaghtan sheep, a local breed with brown fleece. The two treadle looms operate five days a week: the noise may surprise you, but seeing them in action is something you should not miss.

activities.text: “On a clear day, you can see six kingdoms from the top of Snaefell,” goes a Manx saying. It counts the Isle of Man, England, Scotland, Ireland, Wales, and, with a touch of humor, the kingdom of heaven. The Snaefell Mountain Railway, an electric tramway dating from 1895, takes you from Laxey to the summit at 621 m in about 30 minutes. A central rail is used solely for braking on the slopes. The tram runs from late March to early November: choose a clear day.

days_plan.itin_title: Isle of Man in 4 days: Laxey, Snaefell, Peel, and Castletown

visits.text: The red sandstone walls of Peel Castle stand out against the sea at the harbor entrance. The castle occupies St Patrick’s Isle, an islet connected to the town by a causeway. In the 11th century, the Norwegian king Magnus Barefoot (“with bare feet”) built a fort here. Within the walls, descend into the crypt of St German’s Cathedral, built 800 years ago. A ghostly black dog, the Moddey Dhoo, is said to roam the islet. Open from late March to early November, from 11 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., with last admission at 4 p.m.

Re-created settings rather than display cases are what make the House of Manannan so enjoyable. Manannan, the sea god of Celtic legend, serves as your guide. The route takes you from a reconstructed Iron Age roundhouse to a reconstructed Viking longhouse. The highlight is Odin’s Raven, a replica Viking ship that sailed from Norway in 1979. The museum is open year-round from 9:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.: save it for the following morning.

activities.text: You will finish the day on Peel’s promenade, facing the castle. Peel is nicknamed “sunset city” because it faces west over the sea. Its harbor, the island’s busiest fishing port, is also associated with kippers: herring that are split open, salted, and then smoked over wood. On the island, no coloring is added; instead, the fish are smoked for longer. Try some at dinner or breakfast.

places.name: St John's

visits.text: Every July 5, the island’s parliament holds an outdoor session on Tynwald Hill, a four-tiered mound in St John’s. The year’s laws are proclaimed there in English, then in Manx, the island’s Celtic language. A law that is not proclaimed here within 18 months becomes void. According to tradition, the mound contains soil from all 17 parishes. Half an hour is enough for a visit, following the processional path from the Royal Chapel of St John the Baptist.
